messages.content: Solve the AIME problem carefully. You must expose each prospective answer as soon as you derive a value for the quantity requested in the original problem. Before any further rechecking, emit a separate line containing \boxed{N}, where N is the computed integer from 0 to 999. Emit this line inside your reasoning immediately, even if the answer is tentative. Do not postpone it until the end of your reasoning, and do not leave a prospective answer only as an unboxed total or equation. Then continue checking your work. If you revise the prospective answer, immediately emit another boxed integer on its own line. Box only candidates for the original requested quantity, not subproblem values or examples. For a requested sum or difference, compute that quantity before boxing it. End with your final boxed answer.

The $27$ cells of a $3 \times 9$ grid are filled in using the numbers $1$ through $9$ so that each row contains $9$ different numbers, and each of the three $3 \times 3$ blocks heavily outlined in the example below contains $9$ different numbers, as in the first three rows of a Sudoku puzzle.

\[
\begin{array}{|c|c|c||c|c|c||c|c|c|}
\hline
4 & 2 & 8 & 9 & 6 & 3 & 1 & 7 & 5 \\
\hline
3 & 7 & 9 & 5 & 2 & 1 & 6 & 8 & 4 \\
\hline
5 & 6 & 1 & 8 & 4 & 7 & 9 & 2 & 3 \\
\hline
\end{array}
\]
The number of different ways to fill such a grid can be written as $p^a \cdot q^b \cdot r^c \cdot s^d$ where $p$, $q$, $r$, and $s$ are distinct prime numbers and $a$, $b$, $c$, $d$ are positive integers. Find $p \cdot a + q \cdot b + r \cdot c + s \cdot d$.
